articles.title: Far Right Gains Power
articles.author: Vijay Prashad
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Brazil’s general election on 4 October delivered a severe warning to the Left. Flávio Bolsonaro, the presidential candidate of the Liberal Party (PL), finished ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, with approximately 47 per cent against 45 per cent. Neither secured a majority, sending them into a runoff on 25 October. More troubling than this narrow presidential gap was the advance of bolsonarismo through Congress. The election has strengthened a political movement whose ambitions extend beyond defeating Lula to reshaping the institutions that obstruct its exercise of power. The imprisonment (house arrest) and electoral exclusion of Jair Bolsonaro have not dissolved his movement. His son Flávio carries its presidential banner, while other members of the family have won seats in Congress. Michelle Bolsonaro, Jair’s wife, and Carlos Bolsonaro, his son, enter the Senate; Jair Renan, another son, and Renato, Jair’s brother, enter the Chamber of Deputies. Nepobolsonarismo is an appropriate name for this family’s expansion through the state. Yet the family is only the most visible expression of a broader project, rooted in powerful economic interests and a deeply organised reactionary politics. A Presidential Contest with Continental Stakes Lula remains the principal obstacle to the return of this project to the presidency. His defeat would affect workers and peasants throughout Brazil, but also the possibilities for regional cooperation and an independent Latin American foreign policy. Brazil’s size, industrial capacity, raw minerals (such as critical minerals), agricultural resources, and diplomatic reach give its political direction continental significance. A government that subordinates these assets to Washington’s priorities would weaken the space available to neighbouring countries seeking their own paths of development. Related: Netanyahu’s Empty Seats and the Business of Occupation The first-round geography demonstrates both Lula’s strength and his difficulties. He retained a commanding position in the Northeast, while Flávio led across the other four regions. São Paulo’s enormous electorate provided a particularly important advantage to the Right. These divisions cannot be explained by an opposition between an enlightened population and an ignorant one. They require an examination of the different conditions of work, the organisation of political life, and the capacity of competing movements to interpret people’s frustrations. Lula approaches the runoff with a substantial social record. Unemployment fell to 5.3 per cent in the quarter ending in August, the lowest rate for that period in the statistical series beginning in 2012. Such improvements matter enormously to families for whom a regular wage brings relief from daily uncertainty. But an improved national indicator does not settle the political argument. Employment can coexist with exhausting journeys, expensive housing, inadequate public services, and the insecurity of debt. The distance between statistical improvement and lived experience remains terrain on which the Right operates. Bolsonarismo , or Brazil’s far right of a special type, translates these frustrations into resentment against the Left, all public institutions, and vulnerable sections of society. Its promise of order offers an immediate language for fear, while concealing the economic arrangements that produce insecurity. The Left cannot answer this merely by advertising government achievements. It must connect those achievements to a credible programme for changing everyday life, and explain which interests prevent further advances. A worker struggling with debt needs more than reassurance that the economy is performing well. This has been the problem for Lula, whose programme for the future does not seem to promise more than what has been delivered till now. The Senate: A Struggle Over Institutional Power The Senate election is particularly consequential because 54 of its 81 seats were contested. Senators serve eight-year terms, so the results will shape national politics well beyond the next presidential administration. The PL won 19 seats and will hold 28 in the new Senate, making it the largest party. The PT will have nine. The bolsonaristas have therefore established a formidable position, although the PL itself remains short of a majority and must bargain with other parties. Michelle Bolsonaro and Bia Kicis took both seats in the Federal District, while Carlos Bolsonaro and Carol de Toni won the two seats in Santa Catarina. These victories show the movement’s ability to organise coordinated campaigns and concentrate support behind its candidates. There were important successes for the Left: Rui Costa and Jaques Wagner won in Bahia, Humberto Costa retained representation in Pernambuco, and Marília Campos won in Minas Gerais. These results preserve points of resistance within an increasingly hostile chamber. The Senate’s significance extends beyond ordinary legislation. The bolsonaristas have made their confrontation with the Supreme Federal Court a central political objective, including demands to impeach its ministers. Their strengthened representation increases their capacity to pursue that confrontation and to influence the election of the Senate president. Predictions of an automatic majority for impeachment should be treated cautiously: party affiliation, campaign declarations, and votes in a specific proceeding are different things. Nevertheless, the danger of using legislative power to intimidate the judiciary has plainly grown. This is part of a struggle over the conditions under which the far right can govern. The judicial proceedings against Jair Bolsonaro did not remove the social forces supporting him. Those forces now seek greater leverage over institutions capable of restraining them. For the Left, defending democratic space must therefore accompany the struggle to expand social rights. Workers’ organisations cannot afford to lose the freedoms through which they organise, educate, and confront capital. Related: The Donroe Doctrine Comes for Greenland Federal Deputies: the Right Advances, the Left Finds Openings All 513 seats in the Chamber of Deputies were up for election this year. The PL secured 121, consolidating its position as the largest party in this chamber as well as in the Senate. The federation of the Workers’ Party, Communist Party of Brazil, and Green Party won 88 seats, with the PT itself taking 70. The federation’s growth is significant, but it leaves Lula’s allies far from a majority. Parties of the Right hold 303 seats, while the broader parliamentary Left holds 124. The outcome strengthens the far right of a special type within a legislature already dominated by conservative interests. It also weakens some established brokers of parliamentary power, such as the centrão , the collection of parties that trades legislative support for influence over appointments and public resources, although it remains indispensable for majority building. What bargaining will take place within the centrão will now take place alongside a larger and more assertive PL. If Lula wins in the second round, he will confront substantial congressional resistance, but if Flávio wins, the same Congress could facilitate a reactionary programme. Yet the election also brought important representatives of a fighting Left into the Chamber. Jones Manoel, the communist historian elected through PSOL in Pernambuco, received 249,077 votes and finished first in Recife. Elias Jabbour, the communist geographer, was elected for the PCdoB in Rio de Janeiro. Their victories suggest an audience for political education and socialist arguments, even amid the Right’s advance. They offer resources for rebuilding confidence among people who have grown impatient with the narrowing ambitions of parliamentary politics. Jones Manoel has already offered to assist Lula’s runoff campaign, including its digital communication, while proposing stronger attention to demands such as free public transport. This is a useful example of political clarity: criticism of the government’s limitations can coexist with active mobilisation against the far right of a special type. Such unity does not require workers to abandon their demands. It becomes stronger when those demands supply the campaign’s energy and direction. Related: U.S.-China Relations at a Crossroads as Xi Jinping Heads to Washington The Task Before 25 October The runoff cannot be won through negotiations among party leaders alone. It requires organised activity in workplaces, neighbourhoods, universities, and rural communities, with a programme people can recognise in their own lives. Transport, wages, housing, debt, public healthcare, and the time consumed by work must become the substance of a democratic campaign. Defence of sovereignty becomes tangible when it is connected to the ability to use Brazil’s wealth for the needs of its people. The angry tide has advanced, but it has not carried away the millions who still seek another Brazil. The new communist deputies, the surviving mass organisations (especially the landless workers of the MST), and Lula’s enormous electoral base provide foundations for resistance. The immediate task is to defeat Flávio Bolsonaro. The longer task is to build a popular power strong enough to prevent the oligarchy from deciding, election after election, how little change the majority will be allowed. articles.title: UE Hosts Belgian Trade Union Delegation in Pittsburgh
articles.content: On October 3, UE hosted a delegation from the Belgian trade union FGTB. UE Secretary-Treasurer Andrew Dinkelaker and members of UE Local 667 joined the Belgian trade unionists at an Oktoberfest event in Pittsburgh, which raised money for Palestinians. The Belgian union delegation, members of the Belgian FGTB, was on a three-city tour (Minneapolis, Pittsburgh, and Chicago) to meet union leaders and other activists to discuss how they are fighting the far-right and fascism. During the Belgians’ visit, Dinkelaker gave a brief overview of UE’s history and rank-and-file structure. The Local 667 members spoke about their local’s ongoing campaign to boycott Israeli products at the East End Food Coop, where they work. The FGTB is a strong supporter of the Palestinian cause. The delegation was also visiting Pittsburgh because of its rich labor history and the historical connection between the Pittsburgh area and their union. In the 19th century, Belgian trade unionists from the glass industry (the FGTB represents, among other sectors, workers in the glass industry) fled Belgium because they were being persecuted by the anti-worker governments of the time. They settled in the Pittsburgh area, where they established a community of glassworkers. articles.title: Western Region: Take Action to Defend Elections
articles.content: “Our union is a powerful tool that we must utilize to attain a society and a world that is truly equitable and just for all,” declared Local 1186 Vice President Michele McCoy during the Western Region council meeting’s political action report. McCoy and Local 1107 President Kellye Allen were reporting on resolutions that their locals, both located in Wisconsin, had passed about defending labor and democratic rights in the upcoming midterm elections. McCoy also shared how members of her local have been collecting pledge cards in the local and in the community asking working people to pledge to vote for pro-worker candidates and to take action if the Trump Administration moves to interfere in the elections. Zachary Strasberg and Tristan Larkin , Local 1466 and Caedmon Ragland, Local 1498 gave a presentation on efforts their locals, both of which represent graduate workers at public universities in New Mexico, have made to convince their state legislature to adequately fund health care for their members. Local 1122-Northwestern University Graduate Workers President Theo Clifford also gave a report on various political action struggles Local 1122 has been involved in. Following the political action report, the region’s delegates passed a resolution which declared that “the fight to maintain open, free, and fair elections ... [is] an opportunity to bring working people together to build an even stronger force for change in our country and the world.“ Nandell Baines Honored The council meeting opened with a moment of silence for Local 977 President Nandell Baines , who passed away in August . Photos of Baines were displayed on the projector; following the moment of silence Staff Coordinator J Burger , who worked closely with Baines, asked to address the meeting. He told the delegates that Baines "was an amazing person, always tough, always straight with members, [and] hated the boss, always hated the boss.” He recalled how, after Baines had been elected to help negotiate the inclusion of her co-workers under the national UE contract with Hallcon, she arrived at negotiations with a copy of the contract “dog-eared and flagged and highlighted all over”; she “came into the meeting like she was an expert in the contract.” “This union was with her to the very end and gave her something to fight for and she wouldn’t have it any other way,” Burger said. (Baines participated in national bargaining with Hallcon this past summer, even as her health was failing.) “To the very end she was fighting the boss.” “There is no other union out there that fights as hard as this union” UE General President Scott Slawson opened his remarks by recalling how he “was in a very undemocratic union 20 years ago,” one where the national union imposed a contract after Slawson and his co-workers had voted in down. But “when I came to UE, the day I walked in the door, my union steward came and found me. I knew right then and there this was a different union.” The steward invited him to a Local 506 meeting that week, where Slawson witnessed something he had never seen in his previous union: a member made a motion from the floor, which was debated and then voted on, rather than all decisions being imposed from above. “There is no other union out there that fights as hard as this union,” he said, and it is UE's democratic process that fuels that fight, because “we work from the bottom up.” Slawson denounced the “political absurdity” of the current administration in no uncertain terms. “We’re kidnapping world leaders, we’re murdering world leaders, we’re starting unnecessary wars, [and] we’re lining the pockets of the capitalist class,” he said. “We see our money time and time again being handed over to billionaires.” Meanwhile, “people can’t afford medicine, they can’t afford food, they can’t afford to put gas in their cars.” But, he told the delegates, “We can drive change. It takes time, it takes energy, it takes focus, but mostly it takes us. ... Our democracy is being taken from us [but] we have the power, we have the numbers. “It’s time to take oppressive employers on, it’s time to make them nervous. They attempt to distract us because they fear us. They’re afraid of us, and they’re afraid of losing control. It’s time to say in one voice of absolute solidarity, we’ve had enough!” PTI Drivers Find Council Meeting “Really Inspiring” During his remarks, Slawson introduced three rail crew drivers who work for PTI, one of Hallcon’s main competitors. They are part of a large group of PTI drivers nationwide who are seeking to leave their do-nothing company union and join UE. As Karen Warrior put it, “I joined UE because my alleged union UPSEU doesn’t exist.” Becky Holmes explained how the organizing committee is “working hard trying to get everyone involved,” and Jonathan Ziegler said that being at the UE council meeting has been “really inspiring.” Although the workers are potentially facing a long struggle to organize with UE, Ziegler said that UE is working with the committee to recruit and train stewards “so that we have more enforcement, so that we have more protection,” even under the company union contract. Locals “Hard at Work” Organizing and Preparing for Negotiations Beth Miltko of UE Local 1010-New Seasons Labor Union, which represents workers at ten New Seasons Markets in and around Portland, reported that the local is “hard at work” organizing the remaining non-union stores, with a majority of cards signed at one store and majority support at another. “Next time you’ll be seeing them as delegates,” she said, to applause. She also reported on several recent grievance wins, which included restoring jobs for three wrongfully-terminated workers, winning disability accommodations, and reserving unjust discipline. Helene Koumans and Nick Snyder , Local 1043-Stanford Graduate Workers Union, Joe Rathke , Local 1103-GSU at the University of Chicago, and Theo Clifford, Local 1122-NGWU all reported on measures their locals are taking to prepare for their next round of negotiations. (All three locals have contracts that expire in 2027.) Koumans said, “We have a lot to fight for,” and noted that Stanford has already put in writing that they are seeking to overturn Columbia , the National Labor Relations Board decision that gives graduate workers at private universities officially-recognized collective bargaining rights. But Local 1043 is preparing early, having assembled “a team of dedicated organizers and stewards” to serve as their contract action team well ahead of their contract’s August 2027 expiration date. Rathke said that despite the fact that “we’re really facing an existential threat,” Local 1103 is running “full steam ahead on our contract fight,” collecting 1200 responses on an early bargaining survey last spring. “You’re not going to win by rolling over,” he added. “We have to be ready to fight.” Clifford reported that Local 1122 also has contract preparations underway, has conducted a contract survey, and is running a membership drive to prepare for attacks on union security. Ben Lewis and Anna Martin-Boyle , Local 1105-GLU at the University of Minnesota reported that their local is also nine months out from the expiration of their contract, and have also established a contract action team and conducted a bargaining survey, with 600 responses so far. Although as a public university they are not under threat from the possible overturning of Columbia , they are facing “administration-driven austerity,” with their university recently announcing a $225 million budget cut. However, Lewis said, “the money is there,” with the university spending hundreds of millions of dollars on consultants; the crisis is “not a budget crisis [but] a crisis of management.” Delegates from the three Hallcon locals in attendance gave their shop reports together, reporting both on negotiations to renew UE’s national contract with Hallcon and on grievance wins. Lauren Sims , Local 1077, said “they want to give us pennies” but “we’re going to fight until we can’t fight no more.” Erin Frimpong , Local 1177, reported that the locals mobilized over 200 members to join a Zoom bargaining call to put pressure on the company. London Steward , Local 1077, said that attending his first council meeting “is a great experience for me,” and predicted, “I truly believe we’re going to win.” Diana Martinez , Local 1077, and Ray Silva , Local 1477, also addressed the council. New President, Secretary-Treasurer Sworn In At the opening of the meeting, Region President Ramona Malczynski announced that she will be stepping down from her position; the region’s executive board chose Local 1186 President Michael Tomaloff , who currently serves as the region’s secretary-treasurer, to fill out the remainder of her term. They then selected Local 1043 President Liam Sherman to fill Tomaloff’s role as secretary-treasurer, and Beth White , Local 1186, to fill Sherman’s at-large seat on the national union’s General Executive Board. In elections held on Sunday morning, delegates elected Aspen Heintze , Local 1010 and Ray Silva, Local 1477 to fill open seats on the region’s executive board, and Kala Collett , Local 728 and Solé Hall-Hamilton , Local 1498 to serve on the new elections committee that will oversee national officer elections next year. Collett and Hall-Hamilton will join Delores Phillips , Local 1118, who was appointed to chair the committee by the GEB, and Darrion Smith , Local 150, and Andy Vasilik , Local 506, who were elected by the Eastern Region earlier in the month. Following the elections, the new officers, board and committee members were sworn in by General President Scott Slawson. The region also established two task forces, one to review the configurations of subregions and a second to review the region’s process for elections, and approved the use of the region's Member Action Fund to help members attend a Higher Education Labor United conference on AI in Chicago at the end of October.

articles.title: Descent Into Fascism
articles.author: Sharon Kyle, Dick Price, Henry A. Giroux
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. What happens when cruelty becomes a governing philosophy? When political leaders celebrate violence, billionaires wield extraordinary influence over government, and institutions supposedly designed to defend democracy become instruments of repression? These questions were at the center of our recent conversation with political theorist Henry Giroux, whose latest LA Progressive essay, "The Politics of the Abyss: MAGA, Moral Rot, and the Struggle for the Future," examines what he considers the accelerating collapse of America's democratic and moral foundations. Giroux, who holds the McMaster University Chair for Scholarship in the Public Interest, offered an unsparing assessment of contemporary American politics. But our conversation went considerably beyond Donald Trump and MAGA. It explored how the United States arrived at this moment—and whether Americans can imagine and construct a different future. Henry Giroux: Descent into Fascism (30:56) The Collapse of Conscience Giroux began by discussing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his embrace of military power, violence, and the spectacle of punishment. For Giroux, the issue extends beyond individual incompetence or corruption. Hegseth represents a political culture that increasingly celebrates aggression, domination, and authoritarian masculinity. Giroux described the underlying problem as "the collapse of conscience." This moral deterioration, he argued, is reflected not only in the celebration of violence but in the treatment of entire populations as disposable. He distinguished between disposability , in which certain people are denied the resources necessary to live dignified lives, and disappearance , in which people are effectively erased from public recognition, legal protection, and historical memory. Immigration enforcement, attacks on due process, and the normalization of state violence exemplify this larger transformation. Related: The Politics of the Abyss: MAGA, Moral Rot, and the Struggle for the Future But Sharon raised a question that shifted our discussion from political leadership to the American public itself: What does it say about the population that these developments can occur so openly? Giroux's answer pointed toward the institutions that shape public consciousness. How Americans Learned to Accept Authoritarianism "People learn to be racist," Giroux observed. They also learn to embrace ignorance, distrust intellectuals, and accept domination. That learning doesn't occur in a vacuum. Schools, universities, television, social media, and other cultural institutions help shape what people consider normal, legitimate, or desirable. Giroux argued that decades of neoliberalism have encouraged Americans to understand themselves primarily as isolated individuals competing for personal advantage. Under this ideology, self-interest becomes the organizing principle of society, empathy becomes a liability, and solidarity is displaced by competition. "We live in a country that should be appropriately called gangster capitalism," he declared. And, in his formulation, gangster capitalism produces a population increasingly accustomed to its values. The Powell Memo and the Counterrevolution Against the 1960s One of the most revealing exchanges occurred when Sharon raised the 1971 Powell Memo, written by corporate attorney Lewis Powell shortly before his appointment to the Supreme Court. She situated the memorandum within a much longer American history of racial domination, arguing that the reaction against the civil rights, women's liberation, and antiwar movements represented an effort to restore forms of power those movements had begun to challenge. Giroux agreed but added an important distinction. "The Powell memo was the first shot in a counter-revolution," he said. Related: What I Learned Along the Way: Memory, Education,and the Struggle for the Future Its significance, he explained, was that corporate conservatives recognized that maintaining their power required more than government repression. They needed to control ideas. They needed think tanks, influence over universities, and institutions capable of shaping public understanding. The struggles of the 1960s had demonstrated that education could do more than prepare people for employment. It could encourage critical thinking, challenge hierarchy, expand democratic participation, and help previously excluded communities demand power. Conservative elites recognized that possibility as a threat. For Giroux, the subsequent decades witnessed the expansion of a coordinated cultural and political project that increasingly transformed education from a potential instrument of liberation into an instrument of conformity. Today, with artificial intelligence and powerful digital platforms, the reach of those institutions extends into nearly every corner of American life. Will Electing Democrats Be Enough? We asked Giroux whether the United States could experience the kind of fundamental transformation that seemed possible during the 1960s. After all, even if Democrats regain control of Congress or the presidency, wouldn't something much deeper have to change? Giroux was emphatic. "The Democrats may win Congress. But it doesn't mean much really if ... the Schumers of the Democratic Party control Congress," he argued. His criticism extended beyond electoral tactics to the party's relationship with capitalism, militarism, and concentrated wealth. He identified Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and younger political movements as signs that important changes may be underway. Related: From Monsters to Machinery: How Fascism Is Made Particularly encouraging, he said, is the growing willingness of young Americans to consider socialism and reject the anticommunist rhetoric that shaped earlier generations. The possibilities for transformation exist, he suggested, but they cannot be reduced to replacing one set of elected officials with another. Hope Requires Political Action Perhaps Giroux's most important observation concerned hope. Sharon noted that many Americans, particularly those historically excluded from meaningful democratic participation, never fully accepted the claim that the United States was a democracy in the first place. Giroux acknowledged that history but warned against abandoning hope altogether. "I don't see how agency can exist without hope and hope can exist without agency," he said. Without the capacity to imagine a different future, people risk accepting the existing political order as inevitable. He pointed to youth movements internationally as evidence that younger generations are beginning to challenge not merely individual policies but the political and economic arrangements that produce inequality. For Giroux, democratic struggle requires more than outrage and resistance. It requires the imagination to envision something fundamentally different. Our conversation ended on a personal note. Giroux expressed his hope that he might someday return to the United States and participate in gatherings such as our recent Left Coast Forum. For now, he said, he is afraid to cross the border. That admission underscored the seriousness of his warnings. Related: Jason Arday and the Machinery of Racialized Disposability Yet his central message was not resignation. It was that education, political imagination, and collective struggle remain indispensable to the construction of a more democratic future. The question isn't simply whether Americans can defeat Trump. It's whether we can build a society that no longer produces the conditions that made Trumpism possible. Watch our full conversation with Henry Giroux above.

articles.title: Online Pornography Created the Model for Platform Capitalism
articles.author: Patricia Nilsson
articles.content: Online pornography is often seen as a corner of the web that doesn’t bear much analysis. And yet it can hardly be ignored. Firstly, that’s because of the sheer size of the adult-content industry — a sector that in itself is worth around $97 billion annually worldwide and that, at peak times, commands 10 percent of all internet traffic. But more than that, a discussion of its inner workings sheds light on the mechanisms that govern the special kind of attention economy and platform capitalism that we are all wrapped up in. In Guilty Pleasure: The Pornification of the Internet, the Economy, and Everything Else , the journalist Patricia Nilsson discusses porn’s place at the heart of today’s digital ecosystem. As the Financial Times journalist explains, many of the technologies meant to hold and monetize our attention were pioneered by porn sites, and we can even say that digital life in general operates according to the same logic of endless titillation. For Nilsson, “online culture runs on the onanistic logic of porn.” In this new creator economy, everyone is forced to perform a heightened and often openly sexualized version of themselves. In an interview for Jacobin , she spoke to Bartolomeo Sala about what effects this is having on relationships, users, and creators themselves. Bartolomeo Sala You begin Guilty Pleasure by discussing the arguments for and against pornography originating in debates dating back to the 1970s. You relay the criticism, shared by both second-wave feminists and conservatives, that porn should be censored, as it demeans women (“porn is the theory, rape is the practice”) and undermines social cohesion. On the other hand, you discuss the experience of sex workers and porn professionals who value it for its emancipatory, transgressive potential. However, you continue by showing how this moral debate fails to consider the specific digital ecosystem in which porn is produced, disseminated, and consumed. Why do you think these old attitudes are no longer sufficient, and what do they miss about the current political economy of the porn industry? Patricia Nilsson That’s a big question. I’ll say two main things. Firstly, if we talk about porn from the perspective of a traditional feminist critique, whether we should be for or against — I think I write at some point in the book that, to this day, we have not resolved what sex actually means to women. That’s the elephant in the room. I find what someone like Ellen Willis has to say very interesting: that women should be formulating their own sexual desires and fantasies and taking part in the world as equal beings. But the reality is that it’s still a world dominated by male experiences. As to whether these debates aren’t really relevant nowadays, I think we’re so focused on sex that we have failed to form a better understanding of what pornography means today. Why is it so shameful, so taboo, to be a sex worker? The idea that you’re selling yourself? What does it mean to be a sex worker in this digital economy, where we have a paradigm of platform labor where we’re all more or less encouraged to monetize our image and to vie for attention online? A lot of these aspects you could see from sex workers, especially cam workers more than thirty years ago: thinking about your online persona and building a virtual self to attract attention and sell a fantasy other people can consume. That is the core of platform labor today. So I think that a lot of the conversations we’re having today about sex work, especially pornography, miss the point that we have a virtual economy that’s now completely dependent on this type of self-exploitation, which goes way beyond the purely pornographic. Bartolomeo Sala The central idea of Guilty Pleasure is that porn, far from “a trivial sideshow,” is a key feature of the platform capitalism that rules every aspect of our lives. Many of the technologies that keep us glued to our devices, and that track, monitor, and analyze each and every one of our behaviors, were pioneered by porn sites. Today most tube sites such as Pornhub and Youporn are owned by a handful of monopolists backed by big finance who, together with payment processors Visa and Mastercard, are ultimately the arbiters of what can or cannot be shown online. Can you tell us a bit more about how the architecture of the attention economy is a product of online porn? Patricia Nilsson When I say that the logic of porn shaped the business model of the internet, I mean that some of the first people who started making money online were making money in pornography. I remember speaking to this guy, who made a lot of money in the ’90s, who told me, “I never wanted to be a pornographer. I just wanted to make money on the internet. Pornography just happened to be the way.” A lot of these early sites were the first ones to play with how to attract huge amounts of people online — to get them to stay for as long as possible and return as often as possible — and how to make money from their attention. Take things like affiliate marketing: when you host a link on your website, and then if someone clicks on it and goes somewhere else, you get paid for it. Fabian Thylmann — the German dude who is known for inventing tube sites’ business model by bringing Wall Street money into it — didn’t build tube sites. What he did was build one of the first affiliate marketing softwares, which essentially enabled tube sites to track people’s behaviors while on the platform. Or, if you look at camming, it pioneered live streaming. It was the place where people first got to experiment with such things as pay-per-minute models, taking people into private rooms, and using prepaid tokens for tipping. These are all driving the business model of platforms like Twitch and TikTok and attracting more and more people into this virtual economy. But camming also brought a completely extraordinary notion of the online persona: the idea that we can be whoever we want to be or whoever the person on the other side of the screen wants us to be. This doesn’t apply just to ourselves but also to how normal it has become to consume others, to consume the image of others. By that I don’t only mean watching porn or following your favorite influencer on Instagram. Everything has become this form of consumption. This is how we date; this is how we follow our friends. I live in Germany now. I used to live in the UK. I know what’s happening in many of my friends’ lives because I’m consuming their feeds. So that’s what I mean when I say that the logic of porn has seeped through the internet and influenced everything. Bartolomeo Sala I think you perfectly replied to my next question, which was about your claim that “online culture runs on the onanistic logic of porn.” Before we turn to the key takeaway of the book, however, I was wondering if you could tell me a bit more about how the modern porn ecosystem reflects the specific brand of capitalism we all live under. You discuss at length, for instance, how the current state of affairs, in which extreme concentration goes hand in hand with lack of accountability, was born out of a specific US federal law, Section 230, which in the name of freedom of speech shields consumer-generated platforms from liability so long as they remove content that’s violent, illegal, or simply uploaded without consent. Can you tell me how all this came about? And how this arrangement, in which the right to censorship comes at the discretion of powerful financial actors, reflects a more general threat to freedom of expression? Patricia Nilsson Just before we get into Section 230, since you have mentioned it, what I mean when I talk about the “masturbatory business model of the internet” is that the entire virtual ecosystem is designed to be masturbatory to the extent that watching porn essentially is satisfying a psychosocial need on your own by staring at content that has been algorithmically engineered to appeal to you. That is what watching porn is today. And that is what being on your phone is today as well. You know, they’re the same thing. Are you familiar with gooning? Bartolomeo Sala Unfortunately yes, I remember the Harper’s story when it came out. Patricia Nilsson It’s not such a crazy thing as it is made out to be. Gooning is the extreme end of a spectrum that we’re all on in one way, shape, or form. That’s what I mean by the masturbatory business model of the internet: what we’re really doing is being caught up in this loop of self-gratification and self-soothing. That’s why we pick up our phones. We want to soothe ourselves. On Section 230 and freedom of expression: I am not an expert on the issue of regulation. I am not “Section 230 ride or die.” I think it’s obvious to everyone that there is something deeply wrong with the online world, and that we need to change it somehow. At the same time, I argue in the book that regulation of the internet has, in many ways, historically been driven by an attempt to regulate pornography, and that has had a lot of unintended consequences. Section 230 was intended to stop private companies from having too much power over what individuals can say. And with the erosion of Section 230, this is exactly what we’ve been seeing. Visa and MasterCard have become the de facto regulators of porn. They don’t want to have this role, but they have it. A couple of years ago, there was a pressure group that pressured them into taking down over ten million videos on Pornhub. Again, you might say, “we shouldn’t have porn uploaded by unverified accounts,” so maybe this is a good thing. But it misses the bigger point that this kind of pressure exists, and private companies can force content to come down this way. And in a world like ours where things are changing very quickly, you may imagine where that leads. Bartolomeo Sala One aspect of porn being algorithmically engineered to keep us hooked is how this loop of “compulsive self-gratification: craving, stimulation, and temporary relief” directly leads to the “extremefication of porn” and the consequent molding of people’s sexual preferences. If the name of the game is keeping your attention as long as possible, it makes sense that your preferences will be algorithmically nudged toward more intense and fetishistic material as novelty wears off and habituation kicks in. However, I am more interested in asking you how these perverse incentives (pun intended) have also led to what you characterize as unprecedented commodification of the self. OnlyFans might be the most notable example of this new creator economy that blurs the distinction between not just pornographic and non-pornographic content but also between work and everyday life, intimacy and its performance. You write, on the subject of “thirst traps,” that “in the platform economy, sexual self-presentation is just another way to craft a personal brand that serves as both a source of validation and a potential revenue stream.” Can you tell me more about this burgeoning economy: the careful staging of authenticity it requires but also the specific kind of alienation and burnout it breeds? Patricia Nilsson There’s a quote in the book from Bryce Adams, where she talks about why she decided to become an OnlyFans performer. She says if TikTok is just full of people, mainly women, performing these overt eroticized selves all the time, then logically, why not just make money from it, if I am going to be constantly performing as my sexual self in this way anyway? I think this is so interesting for two reasons. On the side of the consumer: What happens to us when we are consuming this type of content? Can it actually start replacing reality? I think we’re starting to see that it can. A lot of people who, for whatever reason, have started spending a lot of time online find that nothing in reality can quite match the excitement, vividness, and speed with which they can feel gratified and validated online. And you can see why. If you’re constantly engaged with performers who are excited, optimistic, and positive, then it can feel quite anticlimactic to go out in the real world and have to negotiate real relationships. However, this is something that I saw very strongly in performers as well, people who are choosing to do this sort of work. A lot of people I spoke to who are OnlyFans performers, or do camming, for example, don’t want to have a real job. That is the driver: the idea of having to go to an office every day and seeing people and having a boss and negotiating with colleagues. A lot of people I spoke to describe having deep anxiety or just not feeling comfortable being with people in person. Being an online sex worker and making money by having these mediated online interactions is just so much safer, because they don’t even have to leave their room. In the last chapter, I interviewed a performer called Lizzy Capri, who was a YouTube mini-celebrity before she launched her OnlyFans. She told me that the way she sees the world is that we are all either consumers or performers, and she would much rather be a performer, a creator. She was telling me that if she didn’t have the incentive to film herself doing things and share them, she would often lack the motivation to do anything at all. She would just end up laying on her sofa all day. Bartolomeo Sala This is what is so dystopian about OnlyFans and performers such as Bryce Adams. It’s like the last stage of capitalist subsumption where life itself is turned into eroticized spectacle. Contrary to tube sites, it doesn’t act as a stress valve for our most primal sexual urges. It seems to respond to an all-too-real craving for connection, but it’s ultimately a simulacrum designed to suck us ever deeper in this voyeuristic sort of parasocial intimacy. Patricia Nilsson I think I say in the book that OnlyFans is the marriage of the pornographic undertones of the internet and the influencer economy that has stemmed from it. OnlyFans performers don’t need to learn any new skills. They are just doing the type of platform labor that we have all been taught to do since being children, which is essentially posting pictures of oneself and being “authentic” — and what I mean by that is this particular sort of performing of authenticity. What I found really interesting in the sort of conversations I was having with Bryce was the way she talks about how people are craving a new type of connection. What OnlyFans offers is this feeling that we’re behind the scenes, that we’re ultimately getting to know the real Bryce. Bartolomeo Sala In the book, you purposefully shy away from solutions. In the epilogue, you outline how AI, as the most perfect tool to aggregate and reproduce our darkest fantasies, could suck us ever deeper in this shadow world that thrives all the more as it works as a substitute for the intimacy and connection we lack in real life. Still, you are careful to avoid stoking moral panic over pornography. Sexual mores are porous and ever-changing. You also show how censorship usually ends up damaging creators themselves, who are suddenly deprived of the revenue streams and protections afforded by digital life. What do you think should be the basic tenets of a progressive agenda to get serious about this subject? Patricia Nilsson For the porn industry specifically, I think it’s very difficult, because most of the content that is being consumed in a place like the UK is not made there, especially now that porn production has been almost outlawed. Take the women who, especially before the [Ukraine] war, were flown into Prague. These are not porn performers; these are just civilians who are brought in and told, “Hey, you can make, like, €5,000 in one week.” That is a life-changing amount of money. So people come in, and they do whatever they’re told. A lot of these women, of course, don’t speak Czech or English. But at the core of this issue is the fact that they are not EU citizens. That is why they can’t turn to the police if anything goes wrong. The same thing happens in Colombia, one of the countries where the camming industry is growing absolutely the fastest. It’s completely unregulated, and many of these cam models are being forced to work almost every day. A lot of them would want to come to the West and do other types of work, but they can’t. I think very often we want to say, “Women are being forced into doing this, this is sex trafficking.” There are, of course, cases where women are put in coercive contracts they can’t get out of. But to a very, very large extent, it’s women choosing to do this. So the question becomes: Why are they choosing to do it? This can be extended to why so many people today want to be OnlyFans performers rather than, say, going to university and getting a job or working at an Amazon warehouse. What do these choices say about the choices that aren’t made or can’t be made? All that aside, if you’re concerned about these women who are doing this type of sex work, what you want is legalization. You want the creation of some kind of framework where you can have some kind of standardization of wages and root out exploitative agents and studios. You want to create ecosystems where porn performers and online sex workers can go to the police if something bad happens to them, where they can help each other flag exploitative clients and so on. articles.title: Comeuppance
articles.author: Steve Hochstadt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In the early 1950s, Senator Joseph McCarthy seemed to wield unchecked power. McCarthy was antisemitic, persecuted people he alleged were homosexual, and defended Nazi soldiers who had massacred American prisoners at Malmedy. His political practice was defined by false accusations and Congressional investigation of his political enemies, mostly advocates of left-of-center ideas. In 1954, his authority was shattered by facts from the mouths of Army counsel Joseph N. Welch and Senator Stuart Symington. They followed the lead of Senator Margaret Chase Smith from Maine, who, after she arrived in 1950, immediately denounced McCarthy’s debasement of the Senate into “a forum of hate and character assassination”. His ignominious downfall forever tainted McCarthy’s name. McCarthy’s hatchet-man, Roy Cohn fell, too. Despite Donald Trump’s attempt to revive his reputation, Cohn’s could not be worse: Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark personify him as the “ American Scoundrel ”. McCarthy’s many enthusiastic supporters in both parties, however, including a young Richard Nixon in California, mostly escaped consequences by letting him fall. Nixon seemed to have left that unpleasant past behind when he became President. But he retained the fantasy ideology about threats from within and a personality defined by vindictiveness. His heartless henchmen, Bob Haldeman and John Erlichman, oversaw the “ Enemies List ”, in which political opponents mixed with national figures from media and culture. Nixon used his considerable powers to target them for personal political purposes. His use of the petty criminality of the Plumbers to ensure his reelection in 1972 led to his plunge from the White House to pariah. Related: Two Sides of Trump’s Mouth Haldeman and Erlichman went to jail and then disappeared into private lives of business success. But they too were forever tainted. When Dreyer's Grand Ice Cream put Erlichman in a TV ad in 1987, customers threatened to stop buying their product and the ad was dropped . Public opinion polls over the past 20 years consistently ranked Nixon worst among modern Presidents . Years into his reign of corruption, lawlessness, greed, and inhumanity, Donald Trump still sits on his golden throne of seemingly unchecked power. His amazing capacity for turning colossal failures into fake news, which then became presidential policy, has created belief in too many Americans. But I see his comeuppance on the horizon. After ruling like a king in 2025, Trump’s power has cracked in 2026. Pointers to his fall from grace are piling up. Trump has been fighting his conviction for assaulting Jean Carroll since 2023, but the Supreme Court rejected his appeals. Nearly twice as many Americans believe Carroll over Trump. The history of DOGE, which becomes fuller by the day, will be a central element of Trump’s eventual reckoning. Elon Musk’s claims of billions in savings turned out to be false. The government had to pay billions to employees for not working . Musk’s leadership of DOGE led to a collapse in the value of his company Tesla. The never-ending war against Iran keeps pushing costs of fuel and daily necessities higher without achieving any of Trump’s asserted goals. Incompetence in major policies, such as relations with Canada, and petty issues, like the Reflecting Pool repairs, keep revealing the costs of Trump’s obsessions to America’s standing in the world. The real details of Trump’s last 21 months in office are entering public consciousness in the first flurry of revelations. Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan used inside sources to explain the workings of his corrupt, incompetent, vindictive, and anti-democratic administration. Carol Leonnig and Aaron C. Davis described the vanquishing of the federal legal administration as Injustice . The careful NY Times columnist Thomas B. Edsall wrote , “President Trump’s corruption is unequaled by any previous resident of the White House.” The federal descent into violent repression is over for now. ICE and its administrative leaders have pulled back in the face of determined popular resistance. The level of leadership just behind Trump has been decimated. The shared disgrace of Kristi Noem, Pam Bondi, and DHS more generally add to the mounting swell of failure and ignominy that is descending on Trump. Trumps’ comeuppance is foreshadowed in his surging American unpopularity. The flood of pre-midterm polls may threaten our sanity and credulity, but they tell a clear story about how far Trump has fallen in the popular estimation. Republicans will be electoral losers, but by how much? No matter how many seats the Democrats gain, comeuppance will only come when political reality intrudes sufficiently on popular ideological dogma to energize enough Americans to express disgust at Trump’s administration. As we approach the midterms, resistance to Trump is spreading through American society. Even formerly silent and loyal Republican politicians are speaking up, trying to salvage their threatened careers. Newsweek posted a “ list ” of Republican lawmakers who have expressed opposition to Trump policies, although it is notable for the half-hearted nature of that opposition. Trump fears his future. His exhortation to the crowd in Dallas was an unprecedented presidential display of narcissism, dishonesty, and desperation: “I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States, that loves us so much he can’t even breathe...I don’t care if I’m registered or not. I’m going to try and cheat like hell, like they do”. A very different Congress will exert power next year. Federal violence will be harder to organize. The moment for Trump’s next assault on our still mostly free system is soon. Whether he attempts another use of administration for violent unpopular ends may depend on our society’s readiness to stand up against his threats. After he no longer wields official power, after his henchpeople decide to talk about what they know, after Trump is history, he will live in the dust bin. Neither Natalie Harp nor ALL-CAPS RANTS on Truth Social nor snipers on a tower taller than the Arc de Triomphe can save him now. MAGA is shrinking. Trump slinks into infamy. The facts sank McCarthy and Nixon. Facts will sink Trump. The technical incompetence, endless lies, weird obsessions, and personal corruption will add up to conclusions to be taught in public schools: Donald J. Trump will be ranked among the worst Presidents in 250 years. History is not kind to bad men. Comeuppance is coming. The only uncertainty is when.

articles.title: Ethiopia vs. Eritrea
articles.author: Ann Garrison
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Ethiopia and Eritrea simultaneously severed diplomatic ties on October 1st. It's a perilous situation. If one nation’s army crosses the other's border, it could draw in neighboring nations, creating a regional crisis from the Horn to the Gulf or, one might say, worsening the crisis that already exists with multiple civil and interstate wars. The entire world, knowledgeably or not, is invested in containing this conflict because of its potential to further destabilize the Red Sea, a major oil shipping channel, driving the price of gas even higher and triggering more inflation cascading upward. Before Ansar Allah attacked Red Sea shipping associated with Israel in 2023, an estimated 12% of seaborne oil passed through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea, and the Suez Canal. Eritrea has 700 miles of Red Sea coast and neighboring Ethiopia is landlocked. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed wants a Red Sea port within the internationally recognized borders of Eritrea, which he can only gain by military force unless Eritrea is willing to negotiate away one of its two ports, Massawa and Assab, which it has no intention of doing. Related: Somalia, Somaliland, and Sovereignty in the Horn and Red Sea Region Massawa and Assab Italy ruled Eritrea as a colony from 1890 until British forces defeated Italian troops there in 1941, during the Second World War. Britain then administered the territory until 1952, when the United Nations created a federation with Ethiopia, and Ethiopia annexed it outright in 1962. The Eritrean people felt they had developed a distinct identity during the years of Italian and British rule, and therefore launched a war of independence against Ethiopian rule from 1961 until their military victory in 1991. A UN-supervised referendum in April 1993 produced a vote for independence from Ethiopia, which Eritrea declared on May 24, 1993. Eritrea’s independence left Ethiopia landlocked, separated from the two ports that were part of Italian Somaliland and are now part of Eritrea. Massawa is Eritrea’s northern port. Assab is its southern port, located near the country’s southern edge on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, just across from where Ansar Allah hold the Strait’s Yemeni coast. When Eritrea was annexed to Ethiopia, Assab was Ethiopia’s largest, busiest port, linked to Addis Ababa by the main highway and equipped with a refinery. In the late 1980s it handled roughly 70 to 75 percent of Ethiopia’s seaborne trade, and with Massawa about 93 percent of export-import traffic. During the mid-1980s famine, the port backed up and ships waited at anchor. Massawa was the older Red Sea port and a naval base, serving northern Ethiopia and Eritrea rather than the Addis Ababa corridor. In 1986-87 it handled about 470,000 tons of cargo. By 1988-89 Ethiopian dry-cargo imports through Massawa were only about 18,000 tons, against more than 1 million through Assab. It was still a working port, but its traffic had greatly declined as it became part of a war zone. Massawa was the Ethiopian Navy’s main base; Assab was its secondary base. It had a ship-repair facility and became the last refuge of the fleet after Massawa fell. In May 1991, as Assab fell, Eritrean troops fired on seven ships that sank and the 14 that could still sail fled to Yemen and Saudi Arabia. Eritrea took the coast, and the Ethiopian navy ceased to exist. Addis Ababa either did not or was not able to negotiate a permanent legal right to use the ports before recognizing Eritrea in 1993. Commercial use continued for a few years, then ended with the 1998–2000 border war, when Eritrea closed the ports to Ethiopian cargo. Since then Ethiopia has moved more than 90 percent of its seaborne trade through Djibouti, with some use of Berbera Port on Somalia’s Gulf of Aden coast. For most of the next two decades Ethiopia’s port issues were cost and dependence. Governments under Meles Zenawi and Hailemariam Desalegn treated access though the Djibouti Port as the workable fix. Related: Johanna Fernández: Unrelenting Advocate for Mumia Abu Jamal The 2018 peace deal seemed to open a new path to port collaboration Ethiopia and Eritrea went to war again from 1998 to 2000, and then sustained an undeclared conflict until the 2018 peace deal that inspired the Nobel Committee to award Prime Minister Abiy the Nobel Peace Prize. The much heralded peace promised a new era of regional cooperation and integration. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, and then Somali President Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed, aka Farmaajo, signed the Joint Declaration on Comprehensive Cooperation Between Ethiopia, Somalia and Eritrea , which still resides in the Peace Agreements Database at the University of Edinburgh. The Western-aligned press screamed, in one op-ed after another, that this agreement was the worst thing that had ever happened to the Horn of Africa, even as Prime Minister Abiy arrived in Eritrea’s capital, Asmara, and was met by jubilant crowds celebrating the end of hostilities between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Negotiations to restore Ethiopia’s access to Massawa and Assab began. The International Institute for Strategic Studies reported, “As part of the rapprochement, landlocked Ethiopia will gain access to Eritrea’s Massawa and Assab ports, important gateways to international trade via the Red Sea.” Partnership, including collaborative port use, might have been part of regional integration leading to development throughout the Horn. The two ports were underutilized, and Assab was in disrepair, after Eritrea suffered decades of war, US sanctions, and UN sanctions engineered by the US. What happened? Future historians will likely look up that joint declaration on the Peace Agreements Database and try to tease out the details, the negotiations behind the scenes, which ultimately led to, for one, the emergence of a US proxy war launched in 2020, when the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the longtime US client that had made Ethiopia an “anchor state” in the Horn, attacked the nation’s Northern Ethiopian Command Base, starting the 2020-2022 Northern Ethiopian Conflict that ravaged the country’s northern Tigray, Amhara, and Afar Regions for the next two years. In 2022, Somalia’s President Farmaajo, one of the signatories to the 2018 peace agreement, lost an election that the US obviously wanted him to lose. A deadline for holding an election suspiciously coincided with a deadline for receiving an IMF loan. After the devastating two-year war, when the Ethiopian army was about to claim victory by taking Mekelle, the capital of Tigray, PM Abiy mysteriously stopped the army from going all the way and Mike Hammer, then US Special Envoy to the Horn of Africa, swept in on a US Air Force jet to fly TPLF leader Getachaw Reda off to Pretoria for peace talks with the Ethiopian government. Neither the Eritrean nor Amhara Forces, both of whom had been principle forces in the war, were included in the talks, central issues were not resolved, and the peace agreement was a resounding failure. Now, four years later, Ethiopia is again caught up in a civil war that may be even worse and may draw in neighboring nations. What is most likely to draw in neighboring nations? A war between Ethiopia and Eritrea that threatens the security of the Red Sea. Prime Minister Abiy accuses Eritrea of supporting the ethnic militias who have declared war on the central government. He could conceivably use that as an excuse to fire on Eritrea, claiming to act in accordance with international law, which guarantees the right to self-defense, and then the two countries could be at war yet again. Related: Saudis Form 14-State Coalition to Stop Ansar Allah The real issue, however, which is plain for everyone to see and repeated in headline after headline, is Ethiopia’s determination to reclaim what Prime Minister Abiy calls its historic right to the Red Sea. Egypt, Sudan, Somalia and Saudi Arabia are all aligned with Eritrea, Israel and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) with Ethiopia. Turkey is allied with Ethiopia, but competing with Israel and the UAE for expanding influence and investment in the Horn. Ethiopia has no right to suddenly claim the ports within its neighbors’ internationally recognized boundaries. International law, ripped and ravaged though it may be, is of course on Eritrea’s side. Black Agenda Report

articles.title: Shawn Fain’s Slate Has Swept the UAW Elections
articles.author: Chris Brooks
articles.content: Shawn Fain and the United UAW slate are headed toward a sweeping victory in the union’s internal elections for its International Executive Board. The results will not be finalized for some time, but the unofficial results are unequivocal: United Auto Workers members are overwhelmingly backing Fain and the militant direction he is taking the union. Voter turnout was low, about 10 percent of the total number of active and retired members, and appears to be on track for a lower total vote count than when the UAW held its first direct election of top union officers in 2022. Previously, officers were elected by delegates at the union’s annual convention, a system that helped entrench the ruling Administration Caucus in power for more than seven decades. Fain eked out an upset victory against incumbent President Ray Curry in a runoff election and was officially sworn in as the first directly elected UAW president in March 2023. I worked for him as chief of staff at the UAW from 2023 to earlier this year. Now, three and a half years later, Fain is on track to become the first directly elected president to win reelection. The field was considerably more crowded this time, with more candidates contesting the top officer positions and regional director seats. Fain’s UAW United slate fielded candidates for eleven of the twelve positions on the International Executive Board. Despite heavy opposition, United UAW candidates are winning by overwhelming margins, demonstrating widespread membership support for Fain’s aggressive approach to bargaining and organizing. That support has been earned. Under Fain’s leadership, the UAW’s historic 2023 stand-up strike won record agreements at the Big Three, delivering 25 percent wage increases, eliminating wage tiers, restoring cost-of-living adjustments, securing bonuses for retirees for the first time in decades, winning the right to strike over product commitments, and bringing electric vehicle battery production under the union’s master agreements. The union then institutionalized its aggressive, high-participation approach to bargaining and began rolling it out across the industries it represents, winning life-changing contracts for workers at Daimler Truck, American Axle, Allison Transmission, Cornell University, Rolls-Royce, and other employers. Following the success at the Big Three, the UAW successfully unionized the workers at Volkswagen’s sole US assembly plant in Tennessee, which became the first foreign-owned Southern auto plant to be organized in US history. Volkswagen workers won a first contract earlier this year. The election results also send an unmistakable message to the federally appointed monitor, Neil Barofsky, who Fain and I believe has repeatedly abused the extraordinary power of his office to try to undermine Fain’s reelection chances. Barofsky, an attorney with the law firm Jenner & Block, has publicly accused Fain and me of retaliating against other union leaders in a series of scathing reports. We have vigorously contested those allegations, which we believe are grossly inaccurate and politically motivated. Those reports followed a remarkable confrontation between Fain and Barofsky over the union’s support for a ceasefire in Gaza and opposition to Israel’s genocide against Palestinians. In December 2023, the UAW became the largest union to call for a ceasefire. Following the announcement, Barofsky called Fain, ostensibly in his personal capacity rather than as the federally appointed monitor, to challenge the union’s position. During that call, Barofsky repeatedly suggested that the union’s statements were antisemitic and “crossed a line.” Fain understood the call as an implicit threat from a federal monitor wielding extraordinary authority over the union’s internal affairs. Barofsky subsequently forwarded an email he had received from the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) to the entire International Executive Board, clearly implying his support for concerns raised by the ADL about the growing support for the union’s ceasefire position among locals. These interactions culminated in a heated confrontation at the February 2024 board meeting, where multiple members of the board objected to the monitor’s interference in the union’s political affairs. During that meeting, which was recorded in the official minutes, Barofsky denied saying the call was made in his personal capacity and claimed that he never characterized the union’s position as antisemitic. He also claimed that Fain had dismissed his concerns about the suffering of Jewish people as “bulls — t.” Unfortunately for Barofsky, Fain recorded their conversation. In July 2026, Drop Site News obtained, authenticated, transcribed, and published the recording. The transcript revealed that Barofsky did say he was calling Fain in his personal capacity and that he repeatedly raised accusations of antisemitism. It also showed that Fain’s reference to “bulls — t” concerned Israel’s killing tens of thousands of innocent civilians — not the suffering of Jewish people. Following publication of the recording, Democratic Rep. Rashida Tlaib called for Barofsky’s resignation. Now, despite the monitor’s investigations, public accusations, and extraordinary interventions into the union’s internal affairs, UAW members are delivering a strong vote of confidence in Fain’s leadership. And Fain is already preparing for the next fight. The centerpiece of his strategy for the 2028 Big Three negotiations is winning back pensions and retiree health care for all autoworkers. Building on the historic 2023 agreements, these victories would eliminate two of the most consequential remaining tiers imposed on autoworkers over previous decades. Much was at stake during these elections. The labor movement, as I have argued elsewhere , is in serious crisis. Fain ran for leadership of America’s most powerful industrial union on a platform of taking that crisis seriously by using the UAW’s resources to wage a real fight for working-class people in this country, both within the union and outside of it. It’s why I worked for him for three years. His opponents in this election wanted to return the union to the days when it was rolling over for the bosses and lacked a broader vision for what organized labor can do, even in its weakened state. The message from UAW members coming out of this election is clear: they want their union to keep fighting, keep winning, and keep moving forward. Anyone who cares about building a fighting labor movement should be heartened.
